Game's fun, easy to navigate and interesting to play.
There are a few issues that I had after finishing it:
-Over simplified.
Despite the interesting concept of grabbing data from every source you can find, Orwell kind of undercuts the excitement of finding a piece that fits by highlighting every piece of information for you. I understand that it makes it much easier and faster to gather information, but I also believe it would me much more rewarding to piece together the story without having it practically spelled out for you.
-Too short.
I'm not going to pretend to know how much work has gone into making a game this interesting, but I did only had 3 hours clocked after completing all the chapters. With a concept this expandable I wish there was more to explore, which leads into my next gripe.
-Needs more content.
And to be clear, I don't necessarily mean that the story needs to be expanded. I mean more links, more photos, more ways of getting information and flushing out the world Orwell was designed to protect. I was disappointed when I couldn't explore the profiles and lives of the peers of the people of interest. Or the ability to review footage, to track people through cameras, recorded or live, to better follow someone's real life footprints and not just their digital ones.

TL;DR Orwell's fun, but very short. I'm not sure I would pay full price for it

I do not recommend this game. Here's why.
First of all - it's boring. It really is. Gameplay-wise it offers just web browsing, reading stuff and clicking. Telltale's games do not offer much in gameplay, but at least you can watch pretty nice visuals and be engaged in the story. Here you just click and browse. Click and browse. And then browse and click a bit more. When I want to read (and I love reading) I read books, not games.
Second thing - visuals. Yes, the game's style and interface are aesthetically pleasing. But... first developers show lack of any effort to make the game rich in gameplay, then do the same with graphics. Yes they use nice colors. Yes the font is elegant. But it's easy to see how it was designed to be made quickly and effortlessly with those simple vectors. Perfect square on plain background is also aesthetically pleasant, but it doesn't show any craftsmanship. And yes, the art style is not crucial for game to be good. But it helps. Especially when game lacks in other areas.
And finally - the story itself. Game puts in you in the shoes of government worker. And it feels like work to play this game. And what kind of work is that? Spying on people and playing a god. Nothing to be proud of. Looks like you're the part of totalitarian machine, aimed at controlling the people. Taken straight from the Orwell's "Year 1984". Which is not necessarily a bad idea, but... the people you spy on are as obnoxious as your job and character you play. So which side developers really take? It looked like whether the game will try to convey I am doing something good, or those terrorist I'm trying to catch are "good" - I will be very, very disappointed. The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.

While playing the game, "investigating" people of interest and gathering every piece of information there ever were about them, i started to think of myself.. Of my data that is thrown all the way around the internet.. What if i'm, someday, become a person of interest?
This game really delivers its message in a powerful way.. You play as an investigator.. Part of a project called "Orwell". This project uses a mass surveillance system to track any person of interest.
As an investigator, your only job is to dig into this mine of data called internet, look for any information regarding this person you deem as relevant.. And just add it to this person's profile. An advisor, someone who's not you, will be the one to judge and conclude based on the very information that were provided by you.. So you kind of have a saying into the final verdict by withholding any related information or misleading the advisors with non-related information WHICH is something that greatly influences the shape of the game.. Your decisions do make a huge difference in this game!

The story is amazing with a lot of twists to it.. You start on a relatively easy-to-figure way.. Every decision at the beginning will only look as either black or white.. But a grey area starts to form in later stages.. Much more difficult decisions will be forced against you to make.. And that were your journey will take a great shift... But all in all, the story is truly amazing and powerful.
The general settings of the game are fairly good as well.. The newspapers, the unique characters, the soundtrack.. Everything contributes to the general atmosphere in a decent way!

I would recommend this game to those who are looking for story-driven games and who would love for a game that seriously takes their decisions into account.

I got this game for free on Humble Bundle this past week. I'd been wanting to try it out, but didn't really want to spend the money (I'm broke lol). But I am glad I played it. It's not terribly long, but it does have a level of replayability. If I can get over how personally victimized I feel by it, I'll definitely play it again to see if I can get a more ideal ending!

The game isn't perfect. I found typos and small bugs--I would get red star notifications for "urgent" or "important" infochunks to find in areas of the game I could no longer access, for example, and they would not go away. Some of the mechanics also bugged me, although the game did provide a decent excuse for it in the end. One such mechanic being that relevant information simply pops up on your screen, rather than it being similar to Her Story in that you have to activity enter keywords to find this information. But it somewhat makes up for it in providing irrelevant information, like news stories on film or items on target characters like their favorite colors. And the devs gave you no lack of things to explore and read, which really makes the story even more interesting--as an investigator for crime, is it really important for you to delve into someone's dating app messages, or personal photos? Not always... but I found I ended up doing it anyway.

The game has a strong message but leaves the ultimate meaning ambiguous and up for the player to decide, leaving you with several story paths to take (though it's not easy to see when this is happening. I thought the game was totally linear at first!) that effect your experience with Orwell. I like that it leaves the ultimate message morally gray, since the topic of Big Brother and digital monitoring is such a gray area to begin with.

So, having played it, I think it's definitely worth a play. Maybe buy the game on sale, but I probably have another 5 hours of playtime in the game at least, and a buck an hour for my entertainment is pretty worthwhile to me. I'll definitely be buying the sequel, once I dare submit to more emotional rollercoaster.

Ultimately, my review comes down to one question:  "Would I pay for this?"  The answer is, no I don't think I would.  I can certainly see where this game would appeal to some, but it doesn't to me.  Hence, the negative score.  I don't regret playing it for free, but I don't think I would have been missing out had I not played it.

Orwell is a story game, first and foremost.  It has somewhat non-linear story to tell, where your actions will affect the details of the plot, but it'll otherwise run more or less the same, and you'll have a choice of three or four endings depending on how you do the finale.  The game tries to cover the problem of survellience but... IMO, it misses the mark completely when the tools used to spy are... indept.  More on that later.

The game boils down to reading fictional internet pages, spying on emails, calls, and texts, and snooping on people's computers.  Your goal is to find "important" information, that is pre-highlighted for you, and drag and drop what you feel is important.  The game stresses that you try to pick correct and relevant information but, ultimately, there's no failure state.  Being accurate or inaccurate only affects the plot details, nothing else, and kinda underminds the engagement of what little gameplay there is.

There's major problems with this though.  You're an investigator on a case, but your partner and the tools you're using are inept.  You can supply information, but you're often not allowed to include the context too.  Context is stupid important in real investigations, so it really undermines, well, the whole system.  You'll also come across "conflicting data", sometimes before you've even found the info it conflicts with.  A good investigator would record it all and then review it later and dismiss what's incorrect.  In Orwell?  You have to pick one.  And sometimes you have to pick blindly.  Just... why?  You also cannot collect information on individuals related to the main suspects, something I figure would be rather important.

It'll also leave you wondering one major question:  what sort of security and surveillance dystopia doesn't even have basic information, such as dates of birth and known addresses, already on file?  For a government trying to imitate 1984's Big Brother, they're failing hard at it.  Especially when around 75% of the information you're gathering is from public sources...

This here's the whole problem:  the game tries to make you question whether government observation is good or bad and whether things should be more private.  But then it puts you in the role of a guy who spends a lot of the time collecting publicly posted information and digging up stuff slower than a Google search.  Snooping into calls, computers, and bank accounts is certainly fishy, yeah, but nothing that would be legally off-limits to a police officer with a warrant in Real Life™.  And considering the plot... warrants are totally justified for everyone involved.

Orwell tries, and the story is just interesting enough for a 3-4 hour playthrough.  But... the political discussion just falls flat due to its own gameplay.  And there's games that are much better at hunting down and acquiring your information without highlighting it for you, like the parts of Hacknet focused on snooping.  

IMO:  not really worth the buy.  If you're really curious, try the demo and if you still want it, wait for a sale.
WORTH IT

Orwell greeted me with an opening cinematic which brings you straight to the plot to what Orwell is really about: Big Brother. However, there is not much that is animated in this game, as the idea is pretty straightforward. Orwell is what happens when you take the format of Hacknet (same publisher) and turn it into a universe with choices and consequences resonating from games like the Life is Strange series (also, the artsy visuals). Perhaps it is also no surprise this particular series lasts 5 episodes, or "days" in the Orwell world. 

The one thing I felt was missing from the game was the ease of controller support. There is quite a lot of dragging to be done with the "dtachunks" you use, which makes a mouse more useful. Yet, the interface could have been much more friendly and easier with more shortcuts to sift through all the links to explore. I've made do with a workaround, but it is one point which I'd set it down to 9/10 instead of a 10/10. The rest of the game was pleasing. The plotline dynamics were interesting. There's no "blink and you'll miss it". Orwell is straightforward and simple without the overcomplications, which is what I feel should be an example of what gaming should be about.

Overall, I look forward to the future.

You, are being watched.

A successful interpretation of a glimpse into a reality where "big brother" is watching you, everywhere. Here are some pros and cons for this game.

Pros:
Very good narrative between suspects, especially in interrogations. It feels real.

The Orwell universe: everything from "The Thought" to the "Reader and Listener", the game is well designed in a manner of keeping George Orwell's 1984's legacy running.

The player choices: yes it does matter. For the system Orwell to acknowledge a piece of information over another that contradicts it is up to you. This gives you the feeling that you are in charge of the case. However, there are some parts that you cannot change, and that will make you question the system. As I will point out later as much as this distrusting gameplay aspect is an excellent addition to the gameplay, it also is a plot-hole for me.

Cons:
Too short: for such excellent experience, it obviously is better not to squeeze the last breath out of it, however 5 episodes without a DLC is just too short.

You: the Orwell system is essentially the Big Brother from 1984. 

"Is there someone as the Big Brother?"
"Of course. This system is the Big Brother."
"I mean, is the Big Brother alive?"
"Depends. Are you alive?"

The mentality of "the Big Brother" is that it knows, sees, hears EVERYTHING. Not just the stuff that you choose to believe in. This makes your perspective on the game very contradictory to the principals of the Big Brother. One way the solve this could have been being the guy who works for the system, not the guy who makes the system work. Would love to see a DLC like that!

Conclusion:
Even if you missed the Humble Bundle, this game is still very much worth your money.

Pros:

- Cool concept, especially if you're into 1984 / V for Vendetta esque stories of government surveillance, conspiracies and 
  coverups.
- Gameplay is fun, I enjoyed the thrill in piecing together seemingly unrelated bits of information and collecting details on 
  targets which started to paint a bigger picture of their motivatons/actions
- I like the idea of only gathering information that can be usefull to your investigation, ie. If you post a targets sexual 
  preference, height, weight etc the game basically says "What does that have to do with them potentially being a 
 terrorist?" It's an interesting mechanic, although perhaps underused.
- In terms of the art style, it's clear and uncluttered and pretty nice to look at
- I have a very old PC and it ran just fine, could probably work on a calculator

Cons:

- The story turns to hot garbage right at the end, and you are left feeling like your actions and oberservations were pretty pointless as the game essentially hands you a tiny amount of predetermined endings to choose from. Enormous plotholes and unresolved dead ends.
- The worst part of investigating is monitoring phone calls....because.....each....word....in.....the...conversation....takes...forever...to....appear...and...it...really....breaks....the...rhythm....
Reading through emails and text message converstions is much quicker and easier, I would hate having to monitor phone calls.
-In terms of the grammar, sentence construction and choice of vocabulary, it's pretty obvious the game has been developed my non-English speakers. It's still very very good, but there are a few instances when the writing is very strange or poorly worded and it does tend to break the immersion a bit.

While the idea is interesting, i feel that the execution is somewhat flawed.
The Gameplay is pretty limited, and basically revolves around scrolling through documents/emails and clicking on the highlighted text. Thats it. There is no actual need to "investigate" and learn details and information.

If you are not interested in the story at all then you don't even need to bother reading any of it and you will still be able to finish the game. The few times that you do have to make a choice, it literally tells you which options you have to pick from, rather than requiring you to read and investigate.


*Story Spoilers Ahead*

Regarding the Story, It completely falls flat. It tries to make a statement about the negatives of a Governmental Surveillance State, however, we don't see the supposed awful aspects of the government surveillance

The "protagonists" (if they can be called that), who are fighting against the Government, are terrorists. They don't encourage any sympathy for thier cause, they aren't likable in any way, so you end up wanting the Government to win in the end.

The way the plot is revealed could have been interesting, reading emails, and looking through web documents, but then at the end, you are just given a massive info dump with all the details just spelled out for you.


Overall, this could have been a great game. If the gameplay was more of a game, and less of a way to deliver story, and if the Story was more of an actual story.

As it stands, it doesn't really succeed as either a game, a story, or as a political statement

Orwell is a small indie game that may or may not be good based on what kinds of games the player may enjoy. I will be reviewing the game with a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.

Pro:
     The story is very deep. Imagine watching a murder mystery show, there is alot of plot twists that really makes you wonder things like who really did it since everyone looks guilty. The story is shaped based on the player's decisions on what they consider important or facts. From there the response might be different based on the players decisions.

       Good ambient music. The music is not much but at times it does emphasis the mood that is suppose to be potrayed. In a moment where you discover something shocking the music will change to potray a shocking mood.

        The art is very simplistic. That is not a bad thing by any stretch of the imagination. It is again an indie game but it does remind me of the polygon designs of super hot and that was a decent looking game. The main point is that the visuals do not overly distract the player  from important moments of the game. It allows for a more cleaner visual naritive with it's simplistic design.

Con:
      The game has a few bugs. The main one I faced was moments that the game froze requiring me to ALT+F4 to close the game and continue where I left off. At moments it is possible for the game to have a dialogue box open but on the background there will be an ongoing conversation via texting or calling and it would prevent you from scrolling through the text to properly read it. This is very likely to happen towards the end of the game.

Conclusion:
         The game is pretty good. The stroy did throw me through a few loops. I did not expect a few of these plot twists and playing through the game was exciting to see how the story played out. Unfortunantly replaying is not nearly as great since the story changes are pretty minor at points and lack any worth wild plot twists when going down a different branching path. Ultimatly  I would reccomend this game but mainly to people who enjoy games with a pretty rich story and branching plot decisions like walking dead.
Surprisingly well done, even thought provoking at times and some moments actually got me like "well that was a mistake, fuck"

A wonderful game, and a valuable lesson.
There are times to rush through the evidence and times to take it slow...make sure you slow down before logging off for the next day, lest you miss data you had not previously noticed. Other then that, a remarkable game that will question your ethical code until the very end.
(This game might mean a bit more to you if you have read 1984. If you have heard of it but not read it, I suggest changing that.)

If you can't decide whether you should buy this or not - you probably should. However, I would not recommend this game to anyone without prior interest to it.

Orwell is a great experience for anyone who enjoys reading as a process. While I personally think that some characters are underdeveloped and ending is a fine example of Deus Ex Machina, overall plot is pretty much okay and can be interesting at times. 

Gameplay, if you don't want to check YouTube, is pretty simple - you drag'n'drop pieces of text between two windows. Window on the right shows you info from web, chats and PC's, and window on the left keeps dossiers on game's characters. By deciding, which info to drop to dossiers, you impact story and it's ending.

This, however, is the biggest flaw of the game. A lot of reviews write about "heavy, morally ambigious choices", but in the end all this morality boils down to "Freedom with a-holes vs Order with a-holes, now choose". I couldn't fullheartedly support any of the outcomes, because throughout the story all of the characters became repulsive and I didn't like any of them. And I also felt discouraged by the "sudden truth" in the end - inconsistent wall of text, which plays for 7 minutes.

Art and overall design, however, is very good. Game looks and plays great.

In the end, game is very cool until chapter 5, which feels rushed and ruins the experience. I got it for free from HumBun, so I am not dissapointed, but I probably would be a little sad if I bought it for fullprice. I will push "Recommend" because most of the game is good, despite it's failed (for me) ending.

If you expect a game to engage more than half a brain cell, this isn't for you. If you want to read a boring, heavy-handed, and pseudo-edgy book while click-and-dragging highlighted text that will interrupt your book reading, this is perfect for you.

There's a lengthy playthrough channel on YouTube. If you think the game gets better or has any sort of progression at all, skip to a later episode, it'll still be the same shallow nonsense.
